headline: Supreme Court leaves Maine lobster boat tracking rule in place
dek: The justices declined to hear a Vinalhaven lobsterman’s challenge, ending the current legal fight over GPS devices required on certain federally permitted vessels.
body: The U.S. Supreme Court has declined to hear a Maine lobsterman’s challenge to a state rule requiring electronic trackers on certain federally permitted lobster and Jonah crab vessels. The decision, formally entered Oct. 5, leaves the First Circuit Court of Appeals’ ruling in place and ends the current court case, according to the [Maine Department of Marine Resources](https://mobile.maine.gov/dmr/news/mon-10052026-1200-dmr-response-supreme-court-order). The [Associated Press](https://apnews.com/article/76cec2682aa2f8dfef2486ade2e8ecdf) published additional reporting on the case Oct. 14.

The lawsuit was brought by Frank Thompson, a fisherman from Vinalhaven, and four other lobstermen, according to [Maine Public](https://www.mainepublic.org/business-and-economy/2026-10-05/supreme-court-declines-to-hear-boat-tracking-case-brought-by-maine-lobsterman). They argued that requiring a monitoring device on their boats violated constitutional protections, including the Fourth Amendment’s protection against unreasonable searches and seizures. A federal judge dismissed the case on jurisdictional grounds, Maine Public reported, and the First Circuit later upheld the tracking requirement.

The rule applies to Maine state license holders who also hold a federal commercial lobster or crab trap-gear permit for specified lobster conservation management areas, including areas 1 through 5 and the Outer Cape Cod area. It is not a requirement for every recreational boat or every person who fishes in Maine waters. The department’s [tracker guidance](https://www.maine.gov/dmr/fisheries/commercial/fisheries-by-species/lobsters/trackers) says covered permit holders were required to have an approved device operating before their first lobster or crab trip after Dec. 15, 2023.

The device records a vessel’s time and position once per minute while the boat is moving. When the vessel is tied up, it records time and position every six hours until the vessel moves again, according to the department. The state says the system supplies more detailed information about fishing effort than older vessel-monitoring systems, which generally report locations less frequently and use satellite transmission.

Maine regulators say the information is intended for fishery management and enforcement, not public tracking of individual boats. The Department of Marine Resources says the data is confidential under Maine law and regulation. It also says the tracker and three years of cellular service are supplied at no cost to eligible permit holders through a congressional appropriation. Harvesters can request their own track data through the department’s process, while the department uses the broader data set for management work.

The department’s stated rationale reaches beyond counting where boats travel. Commissioner Carl Wilson said the information will support lobster stock assessments, offshore enforcement and decisions involving protected species and other ocean uses. The department’s tracker materials also connect the program to efforts to understand fishing effort and possible interactions with critically endangered North Atlantic right whales. Those are the government’s purposes for the rule; they do not resolve the privacy and property concerns raised by the fishermen in court.

The Supreme Court’s refusal to take the case does not create a new tracking obligation. Instead, it leaves the existing requirement enforceable while ending Thompson’s appeal. The [Supreme Court docket](https://www.supremecourt.gov/docket/docketfiles/html/public/25-1105.html) identifies the case as Thompson v. Wilson, and the Maine department says the denial brings this litigation to a conclusion. The ruling also means the First Circuit’s decision remains the controlling appellate precedent for the challenge.

For Maine’s commercial lobstermen, the immediate question is compliance rather than another court date. Covered vessels must keep an approved device installed, powered and certified as required by the department’s rules. The broader policy debate is likely to continue through fishery-management discussions: regulators want fine-grained information as the industry responds to changing stocks, whale-protection obligations and offshore activity, while fishermen continue to weigh those goals against the government’s ability to monitor privately owned boats. The court’s order settles the legal challenge for now, but it does not settle that underlying policy debate.
location: Maine lobster fishery and coastal waters
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Supreme Court leaves Maine lobster GPS tracking rule in place
seoDescription: The Supreme Court declined to hear a Vinalhaven lobsterman’s challenge to Maine’s electronic tracking requirement for certain federally permitted lobster boats.
